1. Core Clinical Tension: A 62-year-old HIV-negative female agricultural worker presented with headache, neck pain, widespread maculopapular rash, a large supraclavicular mass, mediastinal adenopathy, and multi-site osteolytic bone destruction (clivus, occipital condyle, and C6 vertebral body fracture) with polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, strongly mimicking an advanced hematologic malignancy (angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma) or metastatic carcinoma, but caused by disseminated Talaromyces marneffei infection secondary to adult-onset immunodeficiency with anti-interferon-gamma autoantibodies.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Stops after transfer to the oncology department, physical examination documenting the rash, tough supraclavicular mass, and coarse lung sounds, and initial laboratory investigations showing leukocytosis, marked CRP/ESR elevation, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, negative HIV/EBV, and admission CT demonstrating mediastinal mass and osteolytic lesions, before bone marrow biopsy, aspirate culture, or BALF metagenomic next-generation sequencing.
3. Differential Distinctions: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) presents in older adults with lymphadenopathy, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, B-symptoms, rash, and reactive T-cell proliferation on initial biopsy, but is ruled out by demonstration of dimorphic fungi on mNGS and culture and resolution with antifungal therapy. Multiple myeloma or osteolytic metastasis presents with bone destruction and elevated CA 125, but exhibits monoclonal protein spikes or malignant cytology. Disseminated talaromycosis in HIV-negative patients is a classic manifestation of adult-onset immunodeficiency mediated by anti-interferon-gamma autoantibodies.
case_prompt: A 62-year-old female agricultural worker with no history of diabetes, immunosuppressive therapy, or recent trauma was admitted to the oncology service with a 2-week history of headache, neck pain, numbness in both hands, and low-grade fevers (up to 37.6 C). Initial evaluation at a local hospital revealed marked systemic inflammation with a white blood cell count of 19.5 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) of 223.1 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 120 mm/h, total protein of 90.3 g/L, and globulin of 54.8 g/L. Computed tomography (CT) at that center demonstrated an irregular mass in the left upper mediastinum, soft tissue nodules adjacent to the aortic arch, and a pathologic fracture of the C6 spinous process. A preliminary incisional tissue sampling of a mass above the left clavicle had revealed reactive lymphocyte proliferation. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable. Empiric antibacterial therapy with piperacillin-tazobactam yielded no improvement, and she was transferred for suspected neoplasm. On admission, vital signs revealed a body temperature of 36.5 C, heart rate of 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 19 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 153/84 mmHg. Physical examination revealed alert mental status, scattered reddish-brown maculopapular lesions over the trunk and extremities (some exhibiting an annular appearance), a 3 x 4 cm tough, non-tender, immobile mass above the left clavicle, and coarse breath sounds in both lungs. Initial admission laboratories showed a white blood cell count of 21.04 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 19.36 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 1.03 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin 100 g/L, platelet count 192 x 10^9/L, D-dimer 6830 ug/L, serum creatinine 138 umol/L, total bilirubin 33.5 umol/L, direct bilirubin 26.2 umol/L, serum albumin 23.1 g/L, serum globulin 55.2 g/L, CRP 351.30 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.75 ng/mL, CA 125 101.9 U/mL, and ferritin 2331.4 ng/mL. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated marked polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (gamma fraction 40.3%), total IgG was 2450.0 mg/dL, and free light chain ratio was normal at 0.80. Screening for HIV and acute Epstein-Barr virus was negative. Admission CT scans demonstrated diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with consolidation and cavitation, an irregular left upper mediastinal mass, and multi-site osteolytic bone destruction involving the clivus, left occipital condyle, and C6 vertebral body.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: High initial suspicion due to mediastinal mass, supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, rash, and an outside biopsy showing predominantly T-lymphocytic proliferation. Ruled out by repeat lymph node biopsy demonstrating non-clonal reactive hyperplasia and definitive microbiological identification of opportunistic fungal infection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: showing lymphocyte proliferation in fibrous tissue, predominantly T lymphocytes, suggesting the need for further lymph node excision to exclude vascular immunoblastic lymphoma.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to cervical spine fracture, multi-site osteolytic bone lesions of the skull base and spine, and elevated CA 125. Ruled out by a normal immunoglobulin free light chain ratio (0.80) without monoclonal spike, and aspiration confirming a purulent infectious etiology.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Immunoglobulin free light chain assay showed: kappa free light chain 89.0 mg/L, lambda free light chain 111.0 mg/L, free light chain ratio 0.80. HIV negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Identification of Talaromyces marneffei by metagenomic next-generation sequencing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, confirmed by positive fungal cultures from neck mass aspirate and blood, coupled with high-titer anti-interferon-gamma autoantibodies confirming adult-onset immunodeficiency.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Two days later (2024-01-12), the NGS results from the BALF showed TM ( Figure 3G ). Consequently, the antifungal regimen was modified, discontinuing voriconazole and meropenem in favor of amphotericin B

editor_comments: Breakpoint set at admission to oncology service and triage labs/CT imaging, before invasive aspirate cultures, bone marrow histology, or mNGS. Zero mention of fungal pathogens or adult-onset immunodeficiency in the prompt. Quotes verified verbatim.
